articles.title: Nations Championship - England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph scores five tries in first cap since 2022 as hosts score 13
articles.summary: Will Joseph scored five tries on his first England appearance since 2022 as Steve Borthwick's side destroyed Japan 78-15 in Saturday's Nations Championship.
articles.body:
Will Joseph (five), Freddie Steward, Ellis Genge, Cadan Murley, Ben Earl, George Martin, Ben Curry, Marcus Smith, Greg Fisilau score tries as England post huge Nations Championship victory, with Eddie Jones' Japan alarmingly inferior in contest; Joseph on first appearance since July 2022

By Michael Cantillon at Allianz Stadium Twickenham

Will Joseph scored five tries on his first England appearance since 2022 as Steve Borthwick's side destroyed Japan 78-15 in Saturday's Nations Championship.

Joseph (five), Freddie Steward, Ellis Genge, Cadan Murley, Ben Earl, George Martin, Ben Curry, Marcus Smith and Greg Fisilau each scored tries on a day when Japan appeared alarmingly inferior to the hosts, copping a 20-minute red card to lock Harry Hockings after just a minute of play.

Indeed, England's points total would even have been 16 greater had eight conversions not been missed off the kicking tee - George Ford missing six, Henry Slade two.

England - Tries: Joseph (1,10,20,25,56), Steward (15), Genge (18), Murley (29), Earl (40), Martin (45), Curry (64), Smith (68), Fisilau (73). Cons: Ford (15,19,41), Slade (57,69). Pens: Ford (8).

Japan - Tries: Dearns (37), Helu (48). Cons: Saito (38). Pens: Saito (14).

Japan scored tries through lock Warner Dearns and replacement prop Opeti Helu, but it was a rather sombre return for former England head coach Eddie Jones to Twickenham, with his side falling well short of professional standards.

The Test could hardly have started worse for Japan: Joseph sprinting and powering clear down the right in acres of space to score inside a minute, and the TMO bringing Hockings' high tackle on Genge to the referee's attention before Ford even took the conversion.

That left Japan down to 14, and by the sixth minute news came from the bunker Hockings' yellow had been upgraded to a 20-minute red.

Two minutes later, England captain Maro Itoje somewhat bizarrely chose to kick for three points off the kicking tee after a scrum penalty, but Joseph soon had his second, collecting a clever Steward grubber-kick angled towards the corner.

Naoto Saito kicked over a 40-metre penalty for Japan to get onto the board, but England had their third try in the 15th minute: Steward finishing after Martin had bulldozed his way forward.

Within moments, Genge stormed over for England's fourth as England cut through at will and he handed off a succession of Japanese defenders, with Joseph completing his hat-trick inside 20 minutes seconds later, flying over in the corner again.

The Gloucester wing continued to show off his pace and power, bamboozling Japan to score his fourth in the 24th minute, before opposite wing Murley slid over for a try in the corner for England's seventh inside half an hour.

With Japan missing out on a try when tighthead Shuhei Takeuchi was held up, the visitors were next to score in any case as Dearns finished strongly from close range.

England had the final say of the first period, however, as a dominant rolling maul saw Earl get in on the scoring act for a half-time score of 49-7.

Into the second half, Ford produced a stunning 50:22 to earn England a five-metre lineout chance - one which they always looked likely to score from, and duly did through Martin.

Japan lock Michael Stolberg then made a break up the middle of the pitch from deep and was caught by Henry Pollock, but England's Luke Cowan-Dickie was sin-binned for playing the ball while offside after the line-break.

It mattered little as Japan overthrew their five-metre lineout, and Joseph soon remarkably had his fifth try of the Test after plucking an intercept and running clear.

When Curry and Smith went over for England's 11th and 12th tries off lineout attacks, England's home support barely cheered, such was the disparity between the two sides.

Replacement back-row Fisilau was then awarded England's 13th try with seven minutes left, despite appearing to be held up, completing the scoring.

'Speechless' Joseph: A very special day for me

England wing and player of the match Will Joseph told ITV:

"Today was, personally, a very special day. I loved every minute of that.

"I loved the way the team moved the ball today. It was a joy to be part of. I'm speechless - it was a pretty perfect day.

"There were a few changes, and it was a short turnaround, but we got together really quickly. The performance we put in today just shows how hard we've been working behind the scenes.

"I'm going to enjoy today, then we'll be in Sunday and get our heads round the All Blacks. That's another challenge I'm looking forward to being part of - if selected!"

'Proud' Itoje: I don't even know how many tries Joseph scored!

"Japan are a tricky team who gave Wales problems last week but we dealt with those problems.

"I'm super proud of our guys - the guys who came in, Archie [McParland] making his debut, Will making his second cap - I don't even know how many tries he scored!

For England, they next face New Zealand in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium Twickenham on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

England's Nations Championship fixtures and results

Japan travel to face Scotland at Murrayfield in Edinburgh for their next Test, also on Saturday November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Nations Championship - Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Hosts display immense defence to pull off first win vs All Blacks since 1953
articles.summary: Wales pulled off one of rugby's biggest shocks of recent times as immense defence saw them to a 35-28 Nations Championship victory over New Zealand - a first against the All Blacks since 1953.
articles.body:
Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Eddie James, Louis Rees-Zammit score tries as Wales stun New Zealand with first win over All Blacks since 1953 in Saturday's Nations Championship; All Blacks narrowed to within seven in second half, but wave after wave of attack repelled by hosts

Wales pulled off one of rugby's biggest shocks of recent times as immense defence saw them to a 35-28 Nations Championship victory over New Zealand - a first against the All Blacks since 1953.

Wales' victory was built on the foundation of some of their best 40 minutes of rugby for some time in the first half, leading 14-0 and 21-7 after tries from scrum-half Tomos Williams, hooker Dewi Lake and tighthead Archie Griffin.

A decision to keep playing deep in the first half instead of kicking out proved costly, though, allowing New Zealand to level the contest by the break via tries from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, No 8 Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo - the last score coming three minutes into dead time at the end of the first half.

Yet, Wales emerged and flew into a big lead again at the start of the second half, scoring converted tries through centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit for a 35-21 advantage.

Peter Lakai quickly narrowed the deficit to seven with an All Blacks try, and the remainder of the contest was played out almost exclusively inside the Wales 22, only for the home side to repel wave after wave of attack, holding New Zealand up three times in-goal.

Wales - Tries: Williams (2), Lake (6), Griffin (24), James (44), Rees-Zammit (48). Cons: Costelow (3,7,25,45,49).

New Zealand - Tries: Ratima (10), Sititi (31), Fineanganofo (43), Lakai (53). Cons: Mo'unga (10,32,44,54).

Wales made an astonishing start to the contest, creating space down the right for Rees-Zammit to chip ahead and Williams to score a try off a kind bounce after just 90 seconds.

Into the sixth minute, Wales had a second try as their early pressure and exuberance gave way to a strong finish from captain Lake, scoring after a rolling maul had made decent ground in the New Zealand 22.

Staring at a 14-0 scoreline, New Zealand quickly woke up to score their opening try in the 10th minute: scrum-half Ratima breaking off a maul to dart over past poor Welsh defence.

Yet, Wales came strong again as centre Max Llewellyn knocked on a chance he should have scored in the 23rd minute, with the hosts maintaining their composure to grab a third through impressive prop Griffin from close range.

Past the half-hour mark, New Zealand hit back again as back-row Sititi fought his way over after another driving maul in the Wales 22.

As the half drew to a close, Wales twice had opportunities to kick the ball off and bring things to the break, but instead played on in search of further points.

It proved a major error when the All Blacks attacked from deep, and kept making ground and offloading until wing Fineanganofo finished by the posts.

When Richie Mo'unga converted, the score was level at 21-21 at half-time, with Wales no doubt disappointed not to be in the lead after their impressive first half.

The home side came out in the second half undeterred, however, building through Rees-Zammit down the right again, and eventually creating space for James to finish in the left corner.

Sam Costelow converted brilliantly for a 28-21 lead, and moments later the Welsh had a fifth try through Rees-Zammit - turning down a kickable penalty in favour of a five-metre lineout, and executing perfectly off the set-piece to score.

With a lead of 35-21, James then made a remarkable tackle on Anton Lienert-Brown to save a try, but it proved little more than a delay of the inevitable as Lakai dived to ground on the line, narrowing the gap to seven points just five minutes after Wales' latest try.

On the hour mark, Sititi was held up over the try-line by Gareth Thomas when a try looked easier to score, before 21 phases of All Blacks attack were ended by a superb Jac Morgan breakdown turnover.

With 15 minutes to play, James Botham held up Asafo Aumua to deny the All Blacks again, before Wales somehow denied the visitors once more after a lengthy stanza of attack gave way to another call of held-up.

The All Blacks kept coming, but Wales' defence proved inspired to get them over the line for a famous, and wholly unexpected, victory.

Wales back row James Botham, speaking on ITV:

"I can't even describe the emotions. 1953 was the last time we beat the All Blacks.

"It's come from belief. The crowd was behind us - I just want to thank the energy and the noise behind us - you were unbelievable.

"It would be rude not to have a celebration tonight!"

Former Wales international Sam Warburton, speaking on ITV:

"To every fan, the 55,000 who put their hands in their pockets to still watch Wales, this will be so sweet.

"We forget what this playing group has gone through. From Grand Slam champions to one of the longest losing streaks for a tier one nation - they were in the pits.

"Proud to be Welsh on a day like today - those players were magnificent."

For Wales, they next face Australia in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).

New Zealand travel to face England at Allianz Stadium Twickenham for their next Test, also on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Wales beat All Blacks for first time since 1953
articles.summary: Wales celebrate a first victory against New Zealand since 1953 with a brilliant 35-28 win to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Tries: T Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 5

Tries: Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons: Mo'unga 4.

Wales celebrated a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years with a brilliant performance to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.

Steve Tandy's unfancied side lifted a nation as they broke a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretched back to 1953.

In a nine-try Nations Championship thriller at the Principality Stadium, Wales led 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21 before they held off New Zealand with a wonderful defensive display in the final quarter, led by flankers James Botham and Jac Morgan and lock Dafydd Jenkins.

The home side produced a stunning start with tries from inspirational scrum-half Tomos Williams and captain Dewi Lake inside the first six minutes.

Prop Archie Griffin also added a first-half try, but New Zealand responded with scores from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, number eight Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo to level the score 21-21 at half-time.

Wales centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit scored early second-half tries before New Zealand flanker Peter Lakai pulled one back.

The remarkable Wales defence followed as they held up the All Blacks three times over the line to stop New Zealand scoring, to evoke wild celebrations.

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

Wales had won the first three games in this fixture in 1905, 1935 and 1953 but have had to wait more than seven decades for the next.

In 1953 the New Zealand dollar did not exist, Cardiff was not the capital city of Wales and tries were only worth three points.

Sections of the New Zealand media had belittled Welsh rugby before the game, while some bookmakers offered odds of 20-1 for a Wales victory.

Legends such as Sir Gareth Edwards, Alun Wyn Jones, Shane Williams, JPR Williams, Barry John and Phil Bennett had never enjoyed success against New Zealand in a Welsh jersey.

Now Tandy's class of 2026 have written their own chapter in Welsh rugby's history.

The 55,152 was the lowest crowd in the 14 matches between Wales and New Zealand at the Principality Stadium. The fans who stayed away will regret it because it was a day to say "I was there".

Welsh rugby has been in the doldrums for so long, on and off the field, but will hope this famous victory can help galvanise the nation.

This was one of the finest performances in Welsh rugby history and a world apart from the display in the 28-21 win against Japan last weekend.

New Zealand might regret failing to take advantage of France's victory against South Africa on Friday night but they still leapfrog the Springboks to top the southern section with one weekend of regular matches remaining.

Fast start for Wales as hosts dare to dream

Wales made four changes to the side that beat Japan, with Taine Basham making his first Test start in four years by replacing injured number eight Aaron Wainwright.

Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb was preferred to Josh Adams, who scored two tries against Japan, while lock Adam Beard and flanker Botham came in for Ben Carter and Alex Mann.

New Zealand made eight starting swaps from the team that beat Scotland 43-21 , with full-back Beauden Barrett handed the Test captaincy for the first time in his 149th international.

New Zealand's haka was the usual piece of theatre as the All Blacks were lit up by a spotlight and Wales in red.

The hosts reacted quickest from the start with prop Nicky Smith winning a turnover before an excellent long pass from Williams released Rees-Zammit.

The wing chipped ahead and Williams, who New Zealand coach Dave Rennie had highlighted as a pre-match dangerman, pounced for the try.

Wales followed this up with a well-worked forward move and captain Lake latched onto a flat Williams pass to crash over.

It was the first time Wales had led New Zealand by 14 points and the home crowd began to dream.

New Zealand bounce back to level the scores

New Zealand seemed shell-shocked but regathered themselves, and Ratima strolled over for an easy try from an attacking line-out.

Rennie stated before the match they needed to eliminate the threat of Morgan at the breakdown, but they failed to do that when the Wales flanker forced a turnover penalty.

This provided the platform for New Zealand-born Wales full-back Blair Murray to release Rees-Zammit, with only good defensive work by Beauden Barrett preventing a try.

New Zealand's defence kept Wales at bay with some important turnovers before a breathless period of play followed with both sides throwing wild passes.

Once matters had settled down, New Zealand made an unusual decision to go for a scrum in the Wales 22 after being given a penalty. This backfired when the visitors were penalised and it provided the hosts with fresh momentum.

The Wales line-out, which broke down against Japan with six throws going astray, was excellent in the opening quarter and provided the foundation for the third try.

After centre Max Llewellyn was initially denied under the All Blacks' posts, prop Griffin popped up for his second try in two weeks.

New Zealand learned from their earlier error by going for an attacking line-out rather than a scrum and Sititi, who was player of the match in this fixture 12 months ago, eventually dived over.

The All Blacks demonstrated their doggedness at the breakdown by forcing two penalties, while the home line-out began to creak with two overthrows.

New Zealand began to grind away and wing Fineanganofo flopped over with Mo'unga's conversion levelling the scores at half-time.

Wales buck history trend to celebrate victory

This was the time we assumed the script would follow the familiar tale of New Zealand pulling away. Wales had other ideas.

The hosts began the second half in the same fashion as the first, with scrum-half Williams again the architect as his long pass allowed James to crash over.

Morgan again tormented New Zealand to force another turnover penalty. Wales decided to go for the try and the decision was justified.

Williams' long pass allowed Rees-Zammit to cross for the fifth try which is the highest amount scored by Wales against New Zealand.

Two tries inside the first six minutes in the first half for Wales. A pair of scores inside eight minutes in the second.

New Zealand again regrouped, with flanker Lakai burrowing over as the All Blacks came within seven points.

Lakai almost inspired a fifth Kiwi try with a fine break but replacement prop Gareth Thomas had other ideas by expertly holding up Sititi over the Wales line, before Botham repeated the feat on hooker Asafo Aumua.

Replacement Wales eight Taine Plumtree gained two important turnovers before Tandy decided to take off his half-backs Williams and Costelow, with Ospreys duo Dan Edwards and Reuben Morgan-Williams tasked to see out the final 16 minutes.

Edwards and Morgan combined to hold up New Zealand for a third time over the line but the All Blacks onslaught kept coming.

Wales dug deep once more, tapping reserves of strength, discipline and concentration to repel that black wave.

The final whistle delivered the win this side and nation have deserved for so long, reducing players and fans alike to tears of joy.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Hamer-Webb; Costelow, Tomos Williams; N Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, D Jenkins, Beard, Botham, Morgan Basham.

Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, D Lewis, Carter, Plumtree, Morgan-Williams, Edwards, Hennessey.

New Zealand: B Barrett (capt); Fineanganofo, Tupaea, Lienert-Brown, Moorby; Mo'unga, Ratima; Bower, Aumua, Newell, S Barrett, Lord, Segner, Lakai, Sititi.

Replacements: Bell, Numia, Tosi, Hannah, E Blackadder, Fainga'anuku, Preston, R Ioane.

Assistants referees: Nic Berry (Australia) & Luc Ramos (France)

Television match official (TMO): Tual Trainini (France)

Foul Play Review Officer (FPRO) : Leo Colgan (IRFU).

articles.title: Beauden Barrett: All Blacks could not get through Wales' brick wall
articles.summary: New Zealand captain Beauden Barrett praises Wales' brick wall defence after the All Blacks are stunned in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Beauden Barrett said it felt like New Zealand were running into a red brick wall after they became the first All Blacks side to lose to Wales since 1953.

Steve Tandy's men created history with a 35-28 victory at Principality Stadium thanks to a stirring defensive effort.

Wales scored five tries - a national record against New Zealand - but it was their effort without the ball that ended a 34-game losing streak against the All Blacks.

The home side made 346 tackles, with lock Dafydd Jenkins topping the chart with 38, and held the New Zealanders up over the line three times in the second half to protect their seven-point lead.

"It felt like a brick wall at times, so you have to give them credit," said full-back Barrett, who captained New Zealand in a Test for the first time.

"You give opportunities for the crowd to come into the game, and we are well aware of that when we come here.

"That's why it's one of the best places to play rugby - it feels like you are playing 16 or 17."

Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

As it happened: Wales claim first win over New Zealand since 1953

Dave Rennie claimed an unwanted piece of history as the first All Blacks coach to lose to Wales in 73 years.

The former Glasgow boss admitted New Zealand "certainly got out-passioned" but had no regrets about his selection.

The All Blacks made eight changes to their starting line-up between their win against Scotland and their trip to England in the final Nations Championship group game.

"We had a good enough side on the field to win, and if you look at the stats, we had plenty of opportunities and the guys created a lot of chances," said Rennie.

"We just weren't clinical enough, and they were very good defensively.

"I have no regret around the side that we picked, as I've talked about previously, there is really good competition for places.

"There's not a lot between certain positions."

Beaten All Blacks climb above Springboks

New Zealand still inched above South Africa, who lost a thriller in France on Friday, into top spot in the southern hemisphere table.

If the All Blacks win with a bonus point at Twickenham on Saturday (14:10 GMT), they will secure top spot before the Springboks' game in Ireland (20:10 GMT).

"It hurts, but you've got to take it on the chin," said Rennie, who took over from Scott Robertson at the start of the year.

"We weren't good enough; Wales were passionate and every time they kept us out, they grew and became harder to break down.

"We've got to be better, we expect a lot more of ourselves, and I need to see a response at Twickenham."

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Captain Dewi Lake believed in All Blacks history
articles.summary: Captain Dewi Lake says he always believed Wales could defeat New Zealand and end the 73-year hoodoo against the All Blacks.
articles.body:
Captain Dewi Lake says he always believed Wales could defeat New Zealand and end the 73-year hoodoo against the All Blacks.

Wales never trailed in the 35-28 victory as they produced a magnificent display to beat New Zealand for the first time since 1953.

Wales had lost the previous 34 matches in the fixture and had odds of 20-1 with the bookmakers before this game.

But Lake says the group thought they could win against a New Zealand team ranked second in the world and would have gone top if they had beaten Wales.

"Of course we did," said Lake. "Sometimes we sit in front of the media and say we can beat them and it's probably a passing comment for some media outlets or people at home.

"It's not for us. We work hard, we have tough conversations, not only players, but coaches and staff.

"There is much hard work that goes on for this group to grow and succeed.

"For it to finally come to fruition and see it on the field makes me so proud."

Lake's sentiments were echoed by head coach Tandy, who said he felt emotional after the win.

"You could see what it means for the the players, nation and supporters," said Tandy.

"It's incredible. We've been wanting some positivity and the players delivered that.

"The overriding emotion is pride for the playing group, the staff and I'm just glad for everyone who represents Wales.

"You always have belief. History tells you something different but I believe in the group.

"They are a special group of people and I can't wait to come in every Monday to work with them."

Nations Championship: Wales end 73-year wait to beat New Zealand - reaction

Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

Lake's half-time team talk galvanises Wales

Wales led 14-0 and 21-7 in the first half before the All Blacks levelled the score at half-time.

That is when New Zealand have traditionally gone away to secure victory, as they did 12 months ago in a 52-26 success, but there was no repeat this time.

"I did love it at half-time with the playing group, listening to them talk to each other," said Tandy.

"The way the skipper spoken about around what's coming from the next 40 minutes was outstanding."

Lake added: "I won't tell you exactly what I said because I think that's a privilege that the group that we're in the room should keep.

"But it was more or less a flashback to 12 months ago when we were in a similar position at half-time.

"We were not quite in the lead or drawing, but there or thereabouts and it was just a reminder of that feeling for us."

Wales responded with two more tries before New Zealand brought back the deficit to within seven points.

What followed was a defensive effort rarely seen by Wales in recent years with Gareth Thomas, James Botham, Jac Morgan and Dan Edwards involved in holding up New Zealand over the home line on three occasions, while there were also two vital turnovers from replacement Taine Plumtree.

The home side made 346 tackles, with lock Dafydd Jenkins topping the chart with 38 and flankers Morgan and Botham not far behind.

The work of Tandy and defensive coaching duo Peter Murchie and Dan Lydiate was rewarded with heart and skill.

"The players were brave but also phenomenal and showed great physicality," said Tandy.

"New Zealand threw everything at us but the boys got what they deserved and in big games you have to hang on."

Final whistle mayhem but attention turns towards Australia

There might have been only 55,152 in the ground, which was the lowest attendance for a Wales and New Zealand fixture at the Principality Stadium, but they roared the home side onto a famous victory.

Lake summed up the events at the final whistle as he was on the sidelines after being replaced.

"It was almost like you were blocked out things, said Lake.

"You heard the noise, but it was like background noise. I think I stopped watching with a minute and 20 seconds left and just waited for the whistle, which I have done before, but this one was different.

"To celebrate with the boys that you work hard with every day, and the coaches that come in and make you better, is an amazing feeling.

Lock Jenkins stated before the game he was asking for Monday off if Wales beat New Zealand, with Tandy's side facing Australia in Cardiff next Saturday.

"We've got to savour moments, because history tells you this doesn't happen very often, and we need to make make sure we enjoy this," said Tandy.

"I'm sure every rugby club out there is going to be celebrating tonight but it's making sure when we come in, maybe Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning, if Daf gets his way, that we're ready to work.

"Because Australia will be a different test."

That can wait as Wales reflect on halting New Zealand's seven decades of dominance over them.

articles.title: England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph scores five as hosts rout Brave Blossoms
articles.summary: Will Joseph marked his comeback after four years out the Test game with a record-equalling five tries as England tore through Japan.
articles.body:
Tries: Joseph 5, Steward, Genge, Murley, Earl, Martin, B Curry, M Smith, Fisilau Cons: Ford 4, Slade Pen: Ford

Tries: Dearns, Helu Con: Saito Pen: Saito

Will Joseph marked his comeback after four years out the Test game with a record-equalling five tries as England tore through Japan and set their sights on New Zealand next weekend.

A teenage Joseph made his debut as a late replacement in a game against Australia four years ago.

Since then he has endured his boyhood club London Irish going bust, an underwhelming spell at Harlequins and the loss of hearing in his left ear after an auto-immune reaction.

But his superb early season form for Gloucester has thrust him back into the international picture and he took his opportunity superbly, showing work-rate and intelligence as well as raw top-end speed.

Four other players - Douglas Lambert, Rory Underwood, Josh Lewsey and Henry Arundell - have scored five tries in a single match for England.

Japan were vastly over-matched, unable to rev up the ball movement and quickfire rucks that have made them a threat to the game's major powers in the past.

With the outcome clear as England raced out to a 32-3 lead inside 20 minutes, the focus sharpened on a number of individuals attempting to press their case alongside Joseph.

Centre Max Ojomoh, making his first appearance since an excellent performance against Argentina 12 months ago, was smart and sharp in midfield.

The Bath man burst into a pocket of space to help set up Joseph's second and his slick hands opened up a corridor of space for his team-mate's gleefully acrobatic fourth as Japan were buried beneath an avalanche of points.

Henry Pollock, afforded only his second start in his eye-catching England career, carried gamely but didn't have the impact he has shown so often off the bench.

Replacement Greg Fisilau's pair of wince-inducing hits and burrowing try added more intrigue to the back-row equation.

And while George Ford sewed together England's backline neatly enough, his failure to convert more of England's early tries won't help his hopes of regaining the 10 shirt on a more permanent basis.

Northampton scrum-half Archie McParland made his debut as a replacement, but a host of front-line names will return next Saturday as England attempt to take down an All Blacks side smarting from defeat by Wales.

'An al'An almost perfect day' - reaction after Joseph scores five tries in thumping win over Japan

Joseph fills Feyi-Waboso vacancy with aplomb

England have targeted fast starts this autumn and they tore into Japan with relish, launching into a pummelling that only let up long after victory was secure.

Joseph, tasked with bringing the pace and power lost with Immanuel Feyi-Waboso's injury, delivered almost immediately.

Feyi-Waboso had a second-minute try chalked off by the Television Match Official in last weekend's win over Australia and when referee Damian Schneider went upstairs after Joseph crossed in similar swift fashion, it looked ominous for the Gloucester man.

There was nothing wrong in England's build-up before he scorched Riku Kitahara and Warner Dearns for the score. Indeed, there was a lot right for the hosts with Pollock making yards and Ojomoh's slick mis-pass opening up space.

Instead Japan second row Harry Hockings had caught Ellis Genge with a shoulder to the head.

Hockings, upright into the collision, was shown a 20-minute red card on review.

His team, who could not cope with England with a full complement, crumbled.

England scored another four tries in the powerplay, as Eddie Jones, who coached England for nearly seven years from 2016, looking increasingly grim-faced in the coaches box.

England's forward power was an obvious edge to exploit.

Genge splattered number eight Jack Cornelsen on a fearsome charge to the line.

Big carries from George Martin and Asher Opoku-Fordjour set up a prime platform for Freddie Steward to bowl over Kitahara for a try.

Ben Earl was at the back of a stampeding driving maul with brought up a 49-10 scoreline by the break, and Martin barged over from short range early in the second half.

Joseph snaffled an interception to grab his record-equalling fifth try, trotting in while his brother and former England centre Jonathan Joseph looked on from his pitchside role as an in-stadium presenter.

Marcus Smith was given a rare chance to run at fly-half after replacing Ford on 57 minutes.

With the game breaking up and replacements disrupting rhythm, it was hard for the Harlequin to impose much of a pattern on proceedings, but he drifted nicely outside an onrushing tackler to get on the scoresheet.

Last year's victory over New Zealand was one of the high points of head coach Steve Borthwick's regime.

England came into the autumn as underdogs for this year's rematch, but the teams' performances this weekend suggest those odds are narrowing, and perhaps flipping in the hosts' favour.

articles.title: Nations Championship - Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Steve Tandy hails 'phenomenal' players after historic win over All Blacks
articles.summary: Steve Tandy branded his players "phenomenal" after their historic Nations Championship win over New Zealand; Wales beat All Blacks for first time in 73 years, ending run of 34 successive defeats
articles.body:
It was the first time since 1953 that Wales could celebrate beating the All Blacks, ending a run of 34 successive defeats in one of world rugby's historically most one-sided fixtures.

On three separate occasions Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors.

"I feel pride for the players, and to see what it means to the supporters," head coach Tandy said. "We have been wanting some positivity, and I think the players delivered that today.

"We knew it was going to be brutal on both sides of the ball, and I thought the intent from minute one was exceptional.

"You always have belief. They are a special group of people, and there will be lots of bumps along the road, but the boys can be super-proud today.

"The players were phenomenal. New Zealand threw everything at us, and it is just an amazing feeling. We have got to savour moments like this.

"This is a real good statement win for us, and we have got to enjoy it, but we have got to keep going and building performances. We have got a massive game against Australia next week."

First-half tries from Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake and Archie Griffin - all converted by Sam Costelow - put Wales in charge, although New Zealand clawed it back to 21-21 as Cortez Ratima, Wallace Sititi and Fehi Fineanganofo all touched down, with Richie Mo'unga booting three conversions.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game, and such an approach ultimately backfired, with Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit adding further Wales scores that Costelow converted.

New Zealand mustered a fourth touchdown from flanker Peter Lakai, yet try as they might, there was no further way over the Wales line as tackle after tackle kept them out.

Wales captain Dewi Lake added: "To put on the field what we did today, to make history, is tough to put into words, but it is nothing this group doesn't deserve for the work they have put in.

"Sometimes we sit in front of the media and say we can beat them, and it is probably a passing comment for some people at home, but it's not for us. You wouldn't believe the work that goes on for this group to go out and succeed.

"The boys dug in hard, a lot of defensive sets, three or four hold-ups over the line. I think I stopped watching with one minute, 20 seconds left and just waited for the whistle! It is an amazing feeling."

Barrett: Wales defence felt like brick wall

Three Wales players - Dafydd Jenkins, Jac Morgan and James Botham - each made more than 30 tackles, and New Zealand skipper Beauden Barrett conceded how tough it had been to break Wales down in the second half.

"It is a tough one to take, particularly when we were building a lot of pressure but couldn't convert into points," Barrett said.

"It felt like a brick wall at times, so you have to give Wales credit. We were a little bit indecisive, we had three hold-ups over the line, and we have got be better at converting those opportunities."

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie, meanwhile, said: "We are massively disappointed. We started both halves poorly and conceded 14 points quickly. We had plenty of territory, and we need to be a lot better than that.

"Credit to Wales. They were really clinical when they got their chances, and they defended for massive amounts and were the better side.

"We got a bit one-dimensional, and that's decision-making under pressure. They ran hard on to the ball, and we struggled to slow it down."

For Wales, they next face Australia in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).

New Zealand travel to face England at Allianz Stadium Twickenham for their next Test, also on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph makes sensational Test comeback
articles.summary: Will Joseph's comeback after four years off the Test scene was worth waiting for. And there was plenty elsewhere to buoy England in a rout of Japan.
articles.body:
Eddie Jones aired a complaint about Twickenham's in-stadium experience when he appeared on BBC Radio 5 Live this week.

"Being a spectator and being told when to make noise is a bit funny," said the Japan boss, objecting to a big-screen request for an increase in volume.

Jones sat stony-faced in the coaching box as the message appeared again in the midst of his team's 78-15 thrashing at England's hands on Saturday.

There was little for him to enjoy on his return to Twickenham, where he was head coach for seven years.

But, for the rest of a capacity crowd, it was a fun one.

With junior tickets on sale at £15, there was a different atmosphere from usual. The decibels were higher, the demographic was younger, the spirits a little lighter.

And England brought plenty of entertainment to the party. Thirteen tries in total, with Will Joseph's five putting him in the centre of the chorus line.

The 24-year-old won his only previous England cap under Jones. Back in the summer of 2022, he was a teenage apprentice taken on tour to Australia and thrust into the second Test as a last-minute replacement.

His promise has taken some time to be fulfilled. He struggled for game time and fitness at Harlequins after London Irish's bankruptcy forced him to move on from his boyhood club.

An auto-immune condition that cost him the hearing in his left ear was one setback at the Stoop.

But, as part of a rat pack of exciting young English-qualified backs at Gloucester this season, he has been superb: a swerving, offloading, game-breaking threat either on the wing or in midfield.

England deployed him out wide, to bring some of the razzle-dazzle that they lost as Immanuel Feyi-Waboso limped out of their autumn campaign.

Reports from Pennyhill Park during the week had suggested Joseph was doing a fine job of replicating Feyi-Waboso's explosive elusiveness.

He certainly did on Twickenham's main stage, finishing chances with the same pace and power.

"He is pretty similar to Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in the way he plays his game," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people."

Joseph's cartwheeling plant of the ball over the line for his fourth summed up his exuberance.

In the aftermath of that score, Japan flanker Ben Gunter put a consoling arm around full-back Kazuma Ueda, who had been comprehensively burned in a race to the corner.

Japan couldn't get near Joseph, whose first try came after just 60 seconds and his hat-trick score in the 19th minute.

"It has been a challenging four years, but I have enjoyed the journey to get back here and I am happy all that hard work I have put in has paid off," he said.

"I have had a taste for it now and I can't wait to do it again."

Nations Championship: Fixtures and standings

Rugby Union Weekly: The greatest win in Welsh rugby history? Will five-try Joseph face All Blacks?

There was another teenage apprentice taken on that tour of Australia alongside Joseph.

Henry Arundell was Joseph's Irish team-mate. His impact on the trip was greater, scoring a try in the first Test and winning his second and third caps in the series.

The following year, while Joseph returned to the club scene, Arundell made his first England start in the Six Nations.

He earned a place in the Rugby World Cup squad and, in a foregone conclusion of a pool match, cantered in for five tries against Chile in Lille.

Arundell was electric against limited opposition. He has yet to convince in sterner Tests.

Joseph still has those to come. A shade slower, but a smidge smarter, he may be better suited to the Test scene.

New Zealand next Saturday, stung by defeat by Wales, would definitely be a step up if Steve Borthwick decides to find out.

There was plenty elsewhere to please the head coach.

George Martin was at his abrasive best. The Saracens second row led England's carry and tackle standings in the comeback performance we have been waiting for since his 14-month injury lay-off ended in May.

Ellis Genge was snorting fire and bruising ribs and Maro Itoje's rejuvenation after a summer off continues.

In the backline, Max Ojomoh was too clever and quick for the Japanese midfield, spotting space either for himself or others.

Henry Pollock, the other point of interest in a much-changed line-up, found it harder to get into the game with ball in hand, but did the dirty work in defence and at the breakdown that some have questioned.

Borthwick will be waiting nervously on news from his medical room this week, with Ollie Chessum, Seb Atkinson and George Furbank hoping to return in time for the All Blacks.

But a fourth win in a row, after five successive defeats, has further buoyed up his regime.

"The team is really starting to play well," he told BBC 5 Live. "The speed and positioning in attack was very good which gave us options to be able to move the ball.

"There was intent to play fast, with all the strengths of English rugby. We've got some really great attacking talent and I think we are seeing that.

"The balance of pass-kick decisions was really good. Ultimately I think one of the main things is the supporters really enjoyed it. The atmosphere was excellent."

Even Jones, who had Borthwick as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and his time with England, managed a smile by the end.

"It kills me that Will Joseph, I gave him his first cap, he scores five tries against me. Now that's not being very loyal, is it?," he joked.

"He's a great kid. He always was going to be a good player."

England will hope he might turn out even better than that.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland overcome Fiji 43-15 ahead of showdown with world champions South Africa next Saturday
articles.summary: Fiji went ahead briefly at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin before Ireland overhauled them to take a 43-15 victory in the Nations Championship; Ireland are now gearing up for a showdown with world champions South Africa next Saturday
articles.body:
The hosts had won all six previous Test matches between the sides but struggled for fluency and briefly trailed during an uncomfortable opening period at a subdued Aviva Stadium.

Robert Baloucoune scored twice in the first half for Andy Farrell's men after quick-fire tries from Fiji pair Josua Tuisova and Peceli Yato overhauled Tommy O'Brien's early opener.

Ronan Kelleher, Andrew Porter, O'Brien and Nick Timoney went over in the second half as Ireland eventually pulled clear to keep alive their hopes of reaching the Nations Championship final.

Ireland are now gearing up for a showdown with world champions South Africa next weekend.

The result over Fiji leaves Ireland level on 20 points with second-placed England in the northern hemisphere standings - a point below leaders France - ahead of next week's mouthwatering clash with the Springboks.

Ireland must now beat ​South Africa and hope France, who host Argentina, and England, who ​take on New Zealand, falter in Saturday's matches to secure a place in the final at Twickenham on ‌November 29.

articles.title: Ireland vs South Africa: Fiji 'did Ireland a favour' before Springboks game - Jake White
articles.summary: Former South Africa head coach Jake White says his Fiji side "did Ireland a favour" in Saturday's Nations Championship match before they face the Springboks in Dublin next week.
articles.body:
Former South Africa head coach Jake White said his Fiji side "did Ireland a favour" in Saturday's Nations Championship contest before the Irish face the Springboks in Dublin next week.

Fiji lost 43-15 to Ireland at Aviva Stadium having frustrated Andy Farrell's side during a closely contested first half.

While Ireland scored 26 unanswered points in the second half, White - who led South Africa to World Cup glory in 2007 - said Andy Farrell's team cannot afford similarly sluggish spells against the back-to-back world champions.

"Well, I think we probably did Ireland a favour today," the 62-year-old said.

"Let me put it that way, because I think Ireland deep down know that if they play like that against South Africa, they're gonna be up against it."

Ireland shake off sluggish start to brush aside Fiji

White, who was appointed Fiji boss last month, was frustrated that his side opted to take a tap penalty instead of a scrum when the game was in the balance.

"I know how South Africa operate and they would've taken that scrum there, they would have backed the fact that they wanted to get [Ireland] a yellow card," said White.

"They would have taken another scrum and another scrum and another scrum, and they wouldn't have worried about the ref making a call about collapsing or early engaging.

"If I'm coaching South Africa and Malcolm Marx is standing there [as captain], there's no way he is going to say, 'we'll take the tap'. There's no way that happens.

"Marx will say, 'let's take the scrum,' or 'we'll kick it out into the corner and we'll take the line-out'. And that's because they back themselves in those situations."

White added: "The five-metre line-outs that we didn't take opportunities in, and the five-metre scrum and tap penalties, South Africa will turn those into points and I'm sure that Andy [Farrell] and the players will be aware of that.

"They [Ireland] have been around a long time, and they know what's coming, and that's probably why he picked the team that he did because he wanted to make sure that they get a little bit more gun-ready for next weekend, because the easiest thing would have been to change the team and then they're probably one game shy of playing South Africa next week."

When White's comments were put to Farrell, the Ireland boss said: "We were just saying in the changing rooms that we learned some good lessons and use them in the right manner for next week."

Farrell also admitted the scoreline flattered his side after they pulled clear having only led 17-15 at the break.

"Pleased to get the win, especially the scoreline, it flattered us a little bit but having said that you've got to work for those points and after 25 minutes you're down by five points against a side that's playing pretty well.

"As far as the physical nature of the game, I thought they were winning collisions, they were good in the air and on the floor, running really physically through the line and the breakdown was pretty good.

"All in all, we need to understand that wins here when you're under a bit of pressure, they're all pretty precious."

While Ireland struggled to shine at times, Farrell was impressed by James McNabney's shorter-than-expected debut.

The Ulster back row came off the bench and made two huge carries before being forced off with a head injury which rules the 23-year-old out of featuring against South Africa.

"He's joking in the changing rooms - he's delighted with himself for the shortest cameo of a first cap," he said of McNabney.

"I reckon it's the best cameo of three-and-a-half minutes or whatever it was on a debut in Irish history really.

"He remembers the two breaks that he made, so he seems in good spirits."

articles.title: 2026 Women's Rugby League World Cup: Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup
articles.summary: Australia blow New Zealand away in the first half, with a hat-trick for Jaime Chapman, to win 34-10 in Brisbane and clinch a record fourth World Cup.
articles.body:
Tries: Chapman 3, Bent, Surgis, Upton Goals: Southwell 5

Jaime Chapman's grin after acrobatically diving over in the corner said it all. Her second try of the match and Australia's third – the World Cup final put to bed inside 15 minutes.

The red-hot Australian winning machine blew New Zealand away in the first half as they cantered to a record fourth World Cup title - and fourth in a row - with a 34-10 victory in Brisbane.

Making light work of the blistering conditions, which necessitated a drinks break in either half and an extended interval, the Jillaroos ran in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one in the opening 35 minutes, including an initial burst of 24 unanswered points and a hat-trick for Chapman.

Record books were consulted at the break, with Australia on course to challenge New Zealand's 58-0 winning margin from the 2003 final. But the two sides neutralised one another during the second period, New Zealand maintaining their record of not conceding after the break at this tournament - and bagging a consolation try - albeit with Australia long out of sight.

The undisputed dominant force in women's rugby league, Australia are now unbeaten in 16 World Cup matches - a run stretching back to July 2013.

Aside from a brief first-half scare against Fiji in the semi-finals, who became the first side for 13 years to open the scoring in a World Cup game against Australia, it has been a serene procession to the title, scoring 306 points while conceding just 30.

Australia beat New Zealand in Women's RL World Cup final - reaction

It was a ruthless first-half performance from the Jillaroos, who capitalised on the field position presented by a succession of errors and ill-discipline from New Zealand- combined with some sluggish defending – for their opening three tries.

Chapman overpowered three defenders on the left wing to open the scoring after just 125 seconds and produced a flying finish from a sharp offload in the same area after Shaylee Bent had sliced through New Zealand's defence from close range for Australia's second.

After Jess Sergis went the length of the field for their fourth, albeit with a suspected forward pass in the build-up, Shannon Mato dived over as New Zealand profited from back-to-back infringements from the hosts.

However, normal service quickly resumed, with Chapman evading multiple tackles as she ran 60 metres to complete her hat-trick before slick handling down the right wing allowed Abbi Church to feed Tamika Upton on her inside for a simple score under the posts.

Head coach Jess Skinner's decision to select Jesse Southwell ahead of Jocelyn Kelleher at stand-off paid off, as she nonchalantly kicked five of her six conversions, including two from the left touchline.

But this was undeniably Chapman's show, with the 24-year-old, who has faced a succession of injuries, including a spinal fracture in February 2025, and media attention on her personal life, named player of the match.

"She's so young - it's quite scary," said captain Isabelle Kelly. "As a centre, your job is to provide for your winger. Every single time she's there, she executes and finishes to such a high standard.

"The fact she was able to get that down with three girls on her is incredible. Once you get her strides going, she's very hard to stop.

"She's had a lot of stuff going on the last few years and she's really stepped up and owned that position."

Australia went completely off the boil in the second half, with Tarryn Aiken - denied by a try-saving tackle from Georgia Hale - producing their only scoring opportunity of note.

New Zealand, to their credit, vastly improved when defending on the front foot but remained frustrating in attack, completing barely half of their sets due to repeated handling errors, loose passing, and a consistent failure to feed stand-off Chantay Kiria-Ratu.

Mackenzie Wiki's 70th minute try was a deserved, if futile, reward for their second-half efforts.

"Mixed emotions - we obviously came with high hopes of playing really well," said New Zealand head coach Ricky Henry.

"It was a game of two halves and that's the frustrating part for us. We were able to get it back together in the second half but it was too little, too late.

"We didn't handle the speed of the game at the start. They got on top and from there, we couldn't regroup and get our rhythm."

Matt's player of the match: Jaime Chapman

Whether it's stealing the show at the Dally M awards or racking up World Cup final hat-tricks, Jaime Chapman simply takes the spotlight every time.

This was a display that highlighted everything good about rugby league; her first try was brute strength, the second showed spectacular athleticism to cartwheel over to score and the hat-trick try was all about sheer pace, burning off flailing attempts from her pursuers to halt her progress.

She threw in a try-saver to boot, on top of 151 metres, three line-breaks and seven tackle-busts.

Chapman is already a superstar within her sport. This performance ought to be the springboard to something more. World-class athlete and marketable talent.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Matt Dawson column - England must embrace favourites tag v All Blacks
articles.summary: In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's emphatic 78-15 thrashing of Japan and looks ahead to their match against New Zealand next weekend.
articles.body:
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's emphatic 78-15 thrashing of Japan and looks ahead to the match against New Zealand next weekend.

I would love to see the England players absolutely bombarded with the favourites tag before their meeting with New Zealand next week.

Perhaps even over-egg it a little bit - I want to see how this side handles it.

At the end of the day, beating New Zealand or South Africa will likely be a requirement if you want to win a Rugby World Cup.

Are England really favourites? Yes, I genuinely believe they are.

While victories over Australia and Japan have been encouraging, it was Wales' epic win over the All Blacks on Saturday that has given me real faith that this England side is good enough to compete at the highest level.

The key question is whether they can play as they have done over the last two weeks while carrying the favourites tag.

England are playing a better style of rugby than New Zealand. I thought the All Blacks' attack, particularly in the second half in Cardiff, was incredibly one-dimensional.

That is nothing for England to be afraid of as their own attack has been very slick this campaign.

New Zealand aren't going to fix those issues in a week, and England should be capable of soaking up that style of attack defensively.

Of course, the All Blacks were missing some frontline players, including Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie, Will Jordan and Jordie Barrett.

However, what I saw during the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series was the Springboks beginning to work out that style of play after losing the first Test.

They went on to win the next three Tests in a row.

Two Tests to turn England into World Cup contenders

Having beaten the All Blacks last year, I don't want England to approach this home fixture with an underdog mentality. This side needs to get used to being a contender.

The next few weeks could prove crucial in determining whether they are genuine challengers at next year's World Cup.

An undefeated autumn, regardless of whether they finish top of the northern hemisphere standings in the Nations Championship, would elevate England to contenders for the Six Nations.

Two weeks ago, England would have been delighted to find themselves in this position. Now, the reward could be two massive Tests against the very best.

They are not at the level of France or South Africa yet. I think those two sides, particularly after Friday's Test match, are still a little bit ahead of everybody else.

However, England have a good chance of facing New Zealand back-to-back over the next two weeks. What an unbelievable opportunity that would be and what a feather in the cap it would represent for this team.

It would not only give the players belief in what they are capable of achieving, but also send a message to the rest of the world that they can beat New Zealand and potentially follow that up with another victory over the All Blacks or South Africa.

They are not there yet, and I'm not suggesting that beating Australia and Japan alone puts them at that level.

These next two weeks present a huge opportunity to show just how far they have come.

Joseph scores record-equalling five tries as England rout Japan

Comeback kid Joseph thrills as England eye All Blacks

Immanuel Feyi-Waboso's unfortunate injury against Australia leaves a spot open on the left wing.

Five tries against Japan certainly puts Will Joseph in contention. Although he played on the right wing, his experience at centre means he should be comfortable on either side of the pitch.

He is a clever defender who understands the game well and looks a real threat that can offer something different with his balanced running game.

Seb Atkinson keeps the number 12 shirt if he is fit, but Max Ojomoh's performance against Japan means I would have no concerns if he is unavailable.

Ojomoh looks like a Test-level 12. He brought a toughness to his game on Saturday that head coach Steve Borthwick has been asking for.

The bench is also an interesting area, I thought Greg Fisilau was excellent against Japan.

I think England have the ability to step things up when they find their perfect number eight.

Fisilau brought a huge level of physicality in defence and was technically very good. The way he got around the field and controlled things at the base of the scrum was also excellent.

Offensively, England have been playing sevens at eight, with Ben Earl and Henry Pollock filling that role for a while.

It would be a bold call to bring Fisilau into the starting side next week, but he has certainly put himself in the equation over the coming months.

The context is that he was playing against Japan with England miles ahead, but I thought he looked like a natural international number eight.

Wales being in England's World Cup pool next year was never going to be an easy prospect.

That statement performance against the All Blacks reminded everyone why it is so important for the northern hemisphere to have a strong Welsh side.

You won't hear many Englishmen say they want to see them being successful, but I do.

Having Wales competing in that atmosphere, and seeing that narrative of success, is hugely important for northern hemisphere rugby.

I have nothing but admiration for the way that squad played and what they have been through over the last couple of years.

It is important we recognise just how big a win that was. It wasn't simply a case of New Zealand having a shocker. Wales stepped up and delivered a fantastic performance.

To achieve something that hasn't been done for 73 years must bring an incredible feeling of relief and disbelief.

There was talk of the death of Welsh rugby, the struggles of the provinces and whether the game would ever recover. It is a perfect example of how quickly narratives can change in Test rugby.

Wales were excellent in the way they fearlessly attacked New Zealand, and England should take plenty of inspiration from that.

A wounded All Blacks side is a scary proposition. England must go into the game expecting them to be back to their very best.

That is the mentality they need to adopt, while also embracing they are favourites for a reason.

Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Alastair Telfer.

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Reality dawns after Wales dared to dream
articles.summary: As Welsh rugby fans wake up on Sunday morning the realisation will dawn on them that Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years.
articles.body:
Did that really happen? Or was it just a dream?

As Welsh rugby fans wake up on Sunday morning the realisation will dawn on them.

It has happened. Wales have finally beaten the All Blacks again.

For the first time in 73 years - after 34 defeats - 19 December, 1953 is now joined by 14 November 2026 as a defining date in Welsh rugby history.

Thousands of young kids will this morning be turning up to rugby training or matches, driven by parents who have a hint of a headache, with this magical day fresh in the memory.

Steve Tandy‘s heroes will always have this moment, with inspirational captain Dewi Lake and player-of-the-match James Botham shedding tears.

“Best day of my life,” concluded Wales centre Eddie James.

It was a result that sent shockwaves throughout Wales but also around the sporting world.

Friends and relatives who had not been in contact for ages messaged each other to revel in or discuss the result.

People reminisced that their parents or grandparents never saw this day.

There was jubilation in Cardiff but also disbelief at the timing and magnitude of the occasion.

Welsh rugby has been in disarray since the end of the 2023 World Cup after so many of the golden generation retired.

The Wales men’s national team slumped to a record 18 straight Test defeats in a winless run that lasted 16 months as the side slipped to a lowest world ranking of 14th.

Tandy had only won four tests in 13 matches, those victories coming against Japan twice, Fiji and Italy. His side had been hammered twice by world champions South Africa without scoring a point and conceding 116.

So when they awoke on Saturday morning hardly anybody outside the camp would have thought this Welsh team would succeed where previous Grand Slam winning sides had failed to topple New Zealand.

There had been hope, even occasional expectation, before previous contests. That was generally not the feeling this time around, as Wales - ranked 10th in the world - took on a New Zealand side that were ranked top before kick-off in Cardiff.

So where does this staggering result stand in Welsh rugby history?

There have been some wonderful days, with Grand Slam successes clinched in Cardiff in 1976, 1978, 2005, 2008, 2012 and 2019.

Then there was the 30-3 drubbing of England in Cardiff in 2013 to clinch the Six Nations title, while Warren Gatland's side defeated the same opponents two years later at Twickenham in the World Cup.

But this is New Zealand. The All Blacks. A Wales win an achievement many thought might never happen again.

Some might question people for celebrating a victory against a New Zealand side that had rested some top players. You will not find many of those in Wales today.

"I have never seen a performance like that from the men in red," said Radio Wales commentator Cennydd Davies.

"They have emptied the tank and created history."

'One of the greatest wins' - Wales stun All Blacks to go from no-hopers to heroes

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

Tandy has created history by becoming the first Wales coach to beat New Zealand.

Wales had no head coach when they defeated the All Blacks in 1905, 1935 and 1953, with David Nash the inaugural appointment in 1967.

Tandy has succeeded where World Cup winning coaches Sir Graham Henry and Steve Hansen failed by masterminding a Welsh success against New Zealand.

Welsh Grand Slam winning coaches like Gatland, Clive Rowlands, John Dawes and Mike Ruddock also could not inspire the feat Tandy has now achieved.

The unassuming man from Tonmawr has had a tough initiation in his first 15 months as an international head coach but has now announced his arrival on the Test stage.

Tandy has had to deal with questions over his selections and coaching style, but nobody could ever question whether he has the backing of the squad or the way he has immersed himself in the job.

Players often reference the way Tandy keeps in touch, whether they are based in Wales or ply their club trade in England.

This squad play both for each other and for Tandy. There was no greater evidence of that than on Saturday.

Tandy has also finally been provided with a permanent back room staff. It is reaping the rewards.

Tandy earned his international stripes as a defence coach with Scotland and the British and Irish Lions.

The arrival of Peter Murchie, who is in his second campaign as defence coach, is starting to pay dividends with former Wales flanker Dan Lydiate providing able support.

Nothing portrayed the evidence of Welsh players commitment to the Tandy cause than the superhuman defensive effort of the final quarter.

Official rugby statistics are often hard to pin down, especially defensive ones.

Different sites produce slightly differing numbers that are often modified over time when games are analysed again.

The official Nations Championship chart confirmed Wales made a record tally of 346 tackles.

Lock Dafydd Jenkins tops the charts at 38, which matches the tally set by France captain Thierry Dusautoir against New Zealand in the 2007 World Cup quarter-final at the same Cardiff ground.

Jenkins was followed by Jac Morgan (31), Botham (30), centre Eddie James (25) and Lake (24).

Wales had the top nine tacklers on the field, with replacement prop Gareth Thomas making 19 in just 26 minutes.

Defence is not built on statistics alone.

The heart and desire was evident in a final quarter where Wales did not concede a try, and New Zealand captain Beauden Barrett remarked afterwards the All Blacks felt they had hit a brick wall.

A final quarter in which the All Blacks were held up over the Welsh line on three occasions following major interventions from flankers Botham and Morgan and replacements Thomas and Dan Edwards.

A final quarter in which James provided a remarkable try-saving tackle and replacement number eight Taine Plumtree secured two vital turnovers.

Traditionally, the All Blacks have eased away in these closing stages. Not on this occasion.

This was a victory for guts and glory, summed up by BBC rugby correspondent Chris Jones who said: "These results don't happen in international rugby these days.

"It can happen in football where you get an early goal and then it’s backs against the wall and you win 1-0.

"In rugby, teams are too powerful and well-drilled, the superior side normally prevails, the resistance eventually breaks and the dam bursts.

“But that didn't happen in Cardiff. The Welsh defence was heroic."

Nations Championship: Wales end 73-year wait to beat New Zealand - reaction

Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo

Attack matches defence in five-star display

The remarkable rearguard resistance is what will live long in the memory, but Wales’ victory was also built on the clinical offensive game most evident at the start of each half.

Wales were never behind in the game as they held leads of 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21.

That was thanks to tries from Tomos Williams and Lake within the first six minutes of the game and a couple more from centre James and Louis Rees-Zammit at the start of the second half.

Prop Archie Griffin also popped up with a score as Wales crossed for five tries, the most they have scored against New Zealand in Cardiff.

The attacking orchestrator was scrum-half Williams, who enjoyed one of his finest games for Wales, with his long passing repertoire in full flow.

Williams was ably assisted by half-back partner Sam Costelow, who has had to endure criticism during his short international career in Wales’ most high profile jersey.

Fly-half Costelow answered those doubts with an assured performance and also kicked beautifully with five conversions.

Rees-Zammit and New Zealand born full-back Blair Murray continually stretched the All Blacks defence, while centre James proved he is a Test match performer.

Attack coach Matt Sherratt will be a happy man this weekend.

A footnote to the day was that the game was played in front of 55,152, the lowest attendance for this fixture at the Principality Stadium.

It was 13,000 fewer than 12 months ago with almost 20,000 empty seats on show.

The fans that stayed away missed out on a magical afternoon as the players produced a performance worthy of a full stadium.

Those in attendance made themselves heard with Barrett stating it felt like New Zealand were facing 16 or 17 players.

“Since I've been here, I've loved what the crowd brings,” said Tandy.

“I believe we've got the best stadium in the world and it is inspiring for our players and supporters being part of that.

“It is what it is. We had 50-odd thousand here but we've got to perform and hopefully we can grow that.

“I see what the boys do in the communities also and how they connect to our people.”

Whether this attracts people to Cardiff next Saturday for a late match against Australia (20:10 GMT) remains to be seen.

Welsh rugby has been divisive in recent years that it was always going to take a remarkable result like this to provide an opportunity to bring opposing factions together.

Welsh rugby’s issues will not be solved by one win.

articles.title: Women's Rugby League World Cup final: Jaime Chapman scores hat-trick as Australia claim fourth title with win vs New Zealand
articles.summary: Jillaroos wing Jaime Chapman scores hat-trick as Australia surge to Women's Rugby League World Cup glory off back of stunning first-half performance vs New Zealand Women; Shaylee Bent, Jessica Sergis, Tamika Upton also score tries; Success is record fourth title for Australia
articles.body:
It was an emphatic win with the hosts running in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns two, to win their fourth-straight World Cup, the most of any team in the competition's history.

The Jillaroos once again asserted their dominance as the best team in the world, orchestrating a first-half blitz with Chapman scoring three tries.

Two of her tries came inside the first 15 minutes, with the Gold Coast Titans winger carrying three defenders with her as she crashed down for a brilliant try in the first three minutes.

Shaylee Bent took advantage of a gap in the New Zealand defence three minutes later, after Tarryn Aiken created a gap in the New Zealand line for the second-row, who sneaked through for Australia's second.

Chapman then took advantage of an overlap on the left flank, with the flying winger diving for the try line to touch down for her second. It was a spectacular finish.

Centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Full-back Tamika Upton, who sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury, also scored a try and now has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

Kelly: Chapman's finishing ability at such young age is 'scary'

Australia Women captain Isabelle Kelly said:

"She's [Chapman] so young - it's quite scary.

"As a centre, your job is to provide for your winger. Every single time she's there, she executes and finishes to such a high standard.

"The fact she was able to get that down with three girls on her is incredible. Once you get her strides going, she's very hard to stop.

"She's had a lot of stuff going on the last few years and she's really stepped up and owned that position."

NZ's Henry: Mixed emotions for us - 'Too little, too late'

New Zealand head coach Ricky Henry said:

"Mixed emotions - we obviously came with high hopes of playing really well," said New Zealand head coach Ricky Henry.

"It was a game of two halves and that's the frustrating part for us. We were able to get it back together in the second half but it was too little, too late.

"We didn't handle the speed of the game at the start. They got on top and from there, we couldn't regroup and get our rhythm."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Dominant Australia defeat New Zealand in final
articles.summary: Australia win a fourth successive Men's Rugby League World Cup, beating New Zealand comfortably in the final in Brisbane.
articles.body:
Tries: Martin 2, Bostock 2, Best, Trbojevic Goals: Munster 4

Same old story. Having started the Rugby League World Cup in unconvincing fashion, Australia once again showed why they are masters of peaking for the big occasion as they defeated New Zealand 32-12 to be crowned champions for a fourth consecutive occasion.

And this was never really close as the green and gold juggernaut pressed repeat on what has become a familiar pattern - and a depressing one for all those that have attempted to stop them since the Kiwis triumphed in Brisbane in the 2008 showpiece.

Despite being outplayed and outmuscled by Stacey Jones' side in an epic opening to this tournament on 15 October, Australia still edged to a 24-22 victory.

And five weeks on from that pulsating contest - perhaps stung by some observers questioning their credentials - Kevin Walters' team delivered conclusive proof that they remain the remain the benchmark for all others to aspire to.

They were simply untouchable in the first-half, with a demonstration of power and quality that carried them into a 24-6 advantage at the break and a long way towards victory - their 23rd successive win in World Cup matches since that loss 18 years ago.

Back on the ground where New Zealand delivered one of the most seismic shocks the international game has ever seen, there was never a moment where history threatened to repeat itself in front of a sell-out 52,500 crowd.

Jones' team admittedly played a part in their own downfall.

Jamayne Isaako's error from the kick-off set the tone and Australia ruthlessly punished it with Liam Martin bundling over to score from their first attack with just 84 seconds on the clock.

While a converted try from the youngest player on the pitch, Casey McLean, briefly brought New Zealand level it was all they had to show from a disappointing first 40 minutes, when they repeatedly gifted Australia possession and field position.

Quick thinking from Reece Walsh and Bradman Best laid on an eighth try of the tournament for Jack Bostock.

Bostock, who was recovering from knee reconstruction surgery this time 12 months ago, has been a revelation out wide for Australia.

The 23-year-old Dolphins winger has excelled in defence and attack under the aerial ball and married it to a penchant for regularly contributing with key tries at the other end of the pitch.

Best then scored and Martin also crossed for his second try to lay further foundations for Australia success before the half-time whistle.

When New Zealand hooker Erin Clark lost the ball in a tackle with the second period just 36 seconds old, Australia inevitably piled on more points.

Kangaroos full-back Walsh, perhaps with his own personal score to settle after Kalyn Ponga was named the Golden Boot winner eon Thursday, was instrumental.

Walsh's wonderful footwork on the right edge left two opponents floundering before he acrobatically offloaded for Tom Trbojevic to score in the right corner.

Much had been made in the build-up to this encounter of the importance of his mouth-watering match-up with his opposite number. But when Ponga threw a wayward pass into touch minutes later when well placed, it left little doubt as to whom had been able to exert more influence on the outcome.

To their credit, New Zealand kept fighting, and Isaiah Papali'i went over for try their efforts deserved.

However, it proved nothing more than a brief consolation with Bostock diving in for his second try - with the party already under way in the stands behind him - to celebrate Australia's record-extending 13th World Cup success.

'We got disrespected' - Walsh and Australia make World Cup point

Australia beat New Zealand to win Men's Rugby League World Cup - reaction

Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup

Matt's player of the match: Jack Bostock

Jack Bostock had a fairytale World Cup by anyone's standards and didn't disappoint in Australia's final victory.

He has the frame to leap for chips and bombs like stars such as Israel Folau or Daniel Tupou used to, he can finish a try and his carries out of backfield were crucial in sparing the forwards valuable recovery time.

When the going has got tough, he has stood up, whether it's being stared down at a Siva Tau or Haka or having to manhandle a big opponent by the line.

He has grown since his recovery from an anterior cruciate knee ligament injury, and applied that to his international football with real results.
